title: Should you buy this instead of resistance bands? (SPRI review)
summary: Compares SPRI handled resistance tubes with looped resistance bands. Bands are better for accommodating resistance on a barbell; SPRI tubes are better for direct exercises like curls, overhead press and pull-aparts because the rotating handles spare the wrists. He advises buying the lightest tube first and notes that bands freeze in very cold garage gyms while SPRI tubes don't.

claims.claim: For accommodating resistance on a barbell, looped bands beat SPRI tubes: they're easier to secure around pegs and a power rack, and good companies state their tension so you know how much load they add.
Some people wrap SPRI tubes under a bench and onto the barbell ends for bench press; he doesn't recommend it because a handle can slip off and put you in danger.
Band exercises such as curls, triceps extensions and face pulls diversify training, feel great on the joints, give a good pump and help stay injury-free.
SPRI handles rotate and move, letting the wrist find its angle; for standing curls and especially overhead press they feel much better than bands, which sit awkwardly in the hand.
SPRI tubes are also great for pull-aparts and shoulder dislocates.
SPRI sellers give arbitrary difficulty colours rather than load, and even the red ones are tough; buy the lightest (yellow) first to avoid getting one you can't use.
In very cold garage gyms (below 0 F) rubber bands freeze stiff and become unusable, while SPRI tubes don't freeze; he ruined a band this way.
SPRI tubes are pricier than bands but last a lifetime, which is why commercial gyms buy them.
